# FIML and auxiliary variables {.unnumbered}

*First raised in [Week 9](../sem/week-09.qmd). Optional.*

## What it is

**Full information maximum likelihood (FIML)** fits the model to every case, using whatever each case has observed. It gives unbiased estimates when data are **missing at random (MAR)**: when the chance of being missing depends on things you have measured, not on the missing values themselves.

The catch is in "things you have measured": FIML can only use information that is **in the model**. An **auxiliary variable** is a variable that predicts missingness or is correlated with the incomplete variables, included in the model only to make MAR plausible, not because it is part of your theory.

## A worked example

In the real-world Student Life file, a quarter of students skipped the wellbeing items, and students who skipped them work more hours of paid work on average (12.5 hours a week against 5.6). Paid work is also linked to lower wellbeing (r ≈ −.18). So the students with missing wellbeing are likely to have lower wellbeing than those who answered.

Mean of WB1 to WB4, after recoding the 9s as missing:

| Method | Mean wellbeing |
|:--|--:|
| Complete data (the clean file: the true value here) | 3.17 |
| Listwise deletion | 3.20 |
| FIML with the wellbeing items only | 3.21 |
| FIML with `work_hours` as an auxiliary variable | 3.17 |

FIML without the auxiliary variable is **no better than listwise deletion**: it has no information about why data are missing. With `work_hours` in the model, the bias disappears. The difference is small here, but it grows with the amount of missing data and the strength of the relationships.

## How to add an auxiliary variable in Amos

1. Tick **Estimate means and intercepts** (Analysis Properties › Estimation).
2. Add the auxiliary variable as an observed variable.
3. Use the "saturated correlates" approach [@graham2003]: correlate the auxiliary variable with every exogenous observed variable, with the error terms of every endogenous observed variable (in a CFA, the item error terms), and with any other auxiliary variables. This leaves the model's own parameters and df unchanged.

In a CFA, step 3 means many arrows. The **Syntax** tab saves time: one line such as `work_hours <> e_WB1` per item.

## Remember

- Choose auxiliary variables before looking at the results: anything correlated with the incomplete variables or with missingness. Including a few extra is generally safe [@collins2001].
- In Amos, modification indices, normality tests and the bootstrap are not available with missing data. Do screening and diagnostics on a complete-case copy, then fit the final model with FIML.
